turns.text:
Two years ago my ex and I agreed in writing that our son gets a smartphone at 13. His exact words were "Agreed. 13." On Saturday, at Felix's 11th birthday party, in front of nine of his friends, Hector handed him a wrapped smartphone. He didn't tell me he was buying it. I found out when Felix unwrapped it. What was I supposed to do, pull it out of his hands at his own party? I told Hector quietly that we'd agreed on 13. He said we'd talk this week. He hasn't called.

In August he asked about revisiting it for the bus, "even a basic one," and I asked to talk once school started. That was the last I heard of a basic phone. He went around me, bought a full smartphone, and sprang it on me at his party.

So at my house it went in my desk. Felix told me his dad was just being nice. On Wednesday I sent it with him to his dad's and told Hector it doesn't come back to my house. I think he wanted to be the hero of the party. I feel steamrolled, and I'm angry.

How do I get him to see that what we agree on has to mean something?

You make the agreement mean something by putting it back in writing and enforcing it at your house. Waiting for him to call, or for him to feel what you feel, leaves the decision where he already put it: done.

Send a short message now. Keep the party, the hero theory, and the anger out of it. Those are real, and they also give him something to argue with besides the agreement.

Something like:

> We agreed in writing that Felix gets a smartphone at 13. In August you asked about a basic phone for the bus, and I said we should talk once school started. That talk never happened. On Saturday you gave him a smartphone at his party without telling me.
>
> At my house the agreement still stands. The phone does not come here. If you want to change what we agreed — a basic phone, or a smartphone before 13 — we decide that together and put the new agreement in writing before anything is bought or given.
>
> Please confirm this week that the age-13 agreement still stands unless we both change it in writing.

That is the whole ask: a written confirmation, not an apology speech. "Agreed. 13." is already a record. This message adds what happened and what you are doing about it.

If he replies, stay on that point. A basic phone for the bus is a separate decision from a smartphone. He can propose one. He does not get to treat the party as the proposal. If he wants to revisit either, the order is talk, write down the new rule, then act.

With Felix, one calm version is enough: you and his dad agreed on a smartphone at 13, so the phone stays at his dad's. His dad being nice and the agreement being broken can both be true. Felix does not need to carry either one. If the phone comes back in his bag, it goes in the desk and returns at the next handoff, with no extra scene.

You will not get him to see it by explaining it better. You get a record he has to answer, and a rule he runs into every time Felix is at your house. If he will not confirm and this is part of a pattern of deciding things alone, that thread — dates, his "Agreed. 13.", the August ask, the party — is what you take to a mediator or look at against your existing parenting plan. The plan is the place an agreement can be given weight beyond whether he feels steamrolled you.

Yes. You agreed he would get a smartphone at 13, and Hector broke that agreement.

He raised a basic phone in August. You asked to talk once school started. He never had that talk. He bought a smartphone anyway and gave it to Felix in front of his friends, so the first you knew of it was the unwrapping. You were not obliged to take it out of Felix's hands at his own party.

Keeping it out of your house matches what the two of you wrote down. Felix can experience his dad as nice and the agreement can still have been broken. Both of those fit the facts.
